newsitem.title: USA: U.S. shuttle blasts off on new mission.
newsitem.headline: U.S. shuttle blasts off on new mission.

text.p: The space shuttle Columbia, spurting fire and smoke, soared off its Florida launch pad on Friday into a clear blue sky, kicking off a 16-day science mission.

Columbia, the oldest of NASA's four orbiters, lifted off from the Kennedy Space Centre on Florida's east coast at 2.20 p.m. EST (1920 GMT), 20 minutes late because of a minor problem sealing the shuttle's cabin.
"Enjoy your on-orbit 'Spring Break'," NASA test director John Guidi, told the seven astronauts shortly before blast off, referring to the traditional U.S. college and school holiday.

The holiday brought tens of thousands of extra spectators out to line the roads around the Florida spaceport. Kennedy Space Centre officials were forced to turn cars away when the official viewing sites filled up two hours before the blastoff.
NASA officials also attributed the larger crowds to the rare afternoon launch. Most shuttles blast off in the early hours of the morning or soon after sunrise.
Among the spectators were moonwalker Neil Armstrong and Mercury astronaut Wally Schirra. Armstrong, who became the first man to walk on the Moon in July 1969, had never before seen a shuttle launch.

Aboard Columbia was Jim Halsell, mission commander and a veteran of two previous space missions. His pilot, Susan Still, making her first flight, was only the second woman to take the shuttle's pilot's seat.
Janice Voss, the payload commander, was responsible for overseeing the mission's research programme. The mission specialists are Mike Gernhardt and Donald Thomas.
Joining the NASA astronauts are two guest scientists specialising in microgravity research, Roger Crouch and Greg Linteris.
"I just can't tell you how fantastic a ride it was for all of us," Halsell said soon after reaching orbit.
About five hours later the astronauts floated into their orbiting laboratory where they will work in two shifts around the clock.
During the 16-day mission they will light more than 200 fires in a specially designed chamber to learn more about how flames behave in space and on earth.
"Fire has been with mankind for God knows how long, but from a scientific point of view we don't understand fire as well as we should," Halsell said.
A fire in February, which filled the Mir space station with choking black smoke, highlighted the dangers of fire aboard an orbiting spacecraft.
Other experiments will attempt to determine the structure of proteins associated with various diseases and develop new, stronger materials.

Columbia's launch was running a day late because engineers had to install thermal insulation missing from pipes in the shuttle's cooling system, a problem that may have gone undetected for more than 13 years.
The shuttle was due back to earth April 20.
